title: Where the largest cheques go
question: Who are the highest-paid outside contractors each organization names on its return, how much of its spending do they take, and are any of them close to the organization or paid by the City in their own right?
finding: The returns name 1,612 different contractors in 1,798 organization-and-contractor pairings. In 30 pairings one contractor took a quarter or more of everything the organization spent in a year, most of all Resilient Strategies LLC at Chinese Progressive Association (100%, $18.3 million). In 34 the contractor's address is the organization's own. In 58 the contractor has the name of one of the City-funded nonprofits in this study, and in 66 the name of an entry on this project's map of warning signs; these are name matches, and where no address joins them the records do not show whether the contractor and the named organization are one organization or two with the same name. 8 contractors are named by five or more City-funded organizations, the most widely named being Armanino LLP (13).
how: Each full return lists up to five independent contractors paid more than $100,000 (Part VII section B), with an address and a description of the service. Pairings are built across every return on file. Share of spending is the contractor's pay divided by the organization's total expenses in that year, in years with $500,000 or more of expenses. Addresses are compared by street number and street name, ignoring suite numbers and post-office boxes, first between the contractor's address and the organization's on the same returns, then against the City's register of business locations for firms of the same name. Contractor names are compared, after removing punctuation and words such as "Inc", with the names of City-funded nonprofits in this study, with every City vendor paid in fiscal 2019 to 2026, and with this project's map of warning signs. Only names that read as a firm or organization are compared: a name of two to four words that begins with a given name, or is made only of name words, seen among the officers on these returns is treated as a person, and people are not matched to anything nor tested for a shared address. A pairing is listed when the contractor takes a quarter of spending, shares the address, is itself a City-funded nonprofit, or carries more than a lead on the map; rows are ordered by how many of those apply, then by money.
limits: Naming a contractor on a return is disclosure, and using contractors is ordinary: builders for a housing developer, a staffing firm, a subcontracted service provider. A contractor that takes most of the spending may simply be how the work is done. A shared address is common in buildings with many tenants, between an organization and its own affiliates, and for medical groups that work inside a hospital; suite numbers are ignored here. Every link to a City payee or to the map of warning signs is a name match, not a confirmed identity. A return lists five contractors at most, so smaller or sixth-ranked ones are invisible. City totals are from the Controller's table of every payment, less loans, district assessments handed over, benefit-plan trust payments and debt service, and include aid that passes through an organization to others. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
